paper_title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.

Keywords: Hyper-Connections, Birkhoff Polytope, large language model, geometry, pretraining Code: https://github.com/Newiz430/cmHC 1. Introduction Hyper-Connections (HC) (Zhu et al., 2025) extend standard residual connections (He et al., 2016) with learnable mixing across multiple feature streams, shown in Figure 1(a). As unconstrained mixing can destabilize signal propagation in deep networks, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) (Xie et al., 2026) constrains the residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. mHC-lite (Yang and Gao, 2026) provides an exact doubly stochastic constraint through learnable convex combinations of permutation matrices. Although these approaches exhibit training stability by doubly stochastic stream mixing, they do not ensure effective information exchange across streams. Traditional methods like mHC-lite do not encourage an interior exploration of the polytope, so the residual matrices remain close to permutation vertex; our moderate contraction encourages interior exploration, while strong contraction may drive the residual matrices toward the uniform barycenter. See Appendix for more related work. Under-mixing. Prior work has observed an under-mixing state in hyper-connections: residual mixing matrices often remain close to the identity, limiting cross-stream interaction (Alimaskina et al., 2026). We further observe that this behavior is not specific to the identity: mixing can remain concentrated near other permutation vertices favored by initialization. In these cases, the streams are more permuted than actively mixed, limiting the expressivity of multi-stream architectures. To address this issue, existing methods have explored the interior of the Birkhoff polytope through different parameterizations of residual matrices (Dandachi and Diggs-Galligan, 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), but they often rely on more involved constructions without strictly guaranteed mixing effect, and their effectiveness is not validated on large-scale model pretraining. This motivates our geometric contraction strategy with provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization: we restrict the access to the permutation vertices and force the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope. We propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), which contracts the polytope into smaller region inside it by replacing permutation matrices with smoothed ones. This strictly guarantees positive mixing while preserving exact double stochasticity. As illustrated in Figure 1(b), the contraction prevents residual mixing from degeneration around the permutation vertices, indicating guaranteed interior exploration. The mixing trade-off. Another important aspect of our work is the revelation of the potential over-mixing issue that, to our knowledge, remains largely unexplored in recent efforts. Although 2 cmHC : Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction they encourage active stream mixing by different constraints and parameterizations, we argue that stronger mixing is not always better, because excessive mixing makes feature streams less distinguishable. As shown in Figure 1(c), the average similarity between streams becomes closer to 1 when the contraction is strengthened. We theoretically show that the cumulative mixing bound depends jointly on contraction strength and the number of contracted layers. We further reveal the butterfly effect of stream mixing: even numerically small contraction affects the stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients, thereby amplifying over-mixing in deep networks. These findings motivate simple but effective strategy in cmHC: we apply moderate contraction only at shallow layers, encouraging early information exchange while allowing near-identity mappings in deeper layers. We validate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC by extensive experiments on GPT-2 and mixture-of-experts at both 6B and 300B parameter scales, showing how the trade-off design achieves lower training loss while stabilizing gradient propagation on extremely largescale model pretraining. Furthermore, despite no new parameterization required, we improve the efficiency of cmHC in industrial scenarios by developing fused operators on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We theoretically and empirically reveal the mixing trade-off in mHC: under-mixing makes hyperconnections degenerate into set of single streams, while over-mixing makes streams less distinguishable from each other. We propose cmHC, an exact doubly stochastic method which performs moderate geometric contraction to the Birkhoff polytope without introducing additional parameters. We evaluate cmHC through extensive experiments from GPT-2 to 6B-MoE and 300B-MoE to validate its effectiveness and scalability, and develop efficient fused operators on Ascend NPUs to support efficient execution. 2. Conclusion We study how manifold-constrained hyper-connections mix information across feature streams. We first reveal that residual matrices in traditional methods tend to stay close to the permutation vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, leading to under-mixing, while excessive mixing can drive streams toward uniform state and suppress their differences. Motivated by this mixing trade-off, we propose cmHC, which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior, providing provable bound on stream mixing without introducing any new parameterization. Our analysis bounds cumulative residual mixing, stream differences and gradient differences of mixing coefficients across layers, showing that the effect of contraction depends jointly on its strength and the number of contracted layers. This motivates simple but effective strategy that applies moderate contraction to shallow layers to prevent over-mixing. Our comparative experiments and analyses of training dynamics from GPT-2 to 6Band 300B-MoE models validate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. Recent progress in large language models has been driven by advances in pretraining, post-training, model architecture, and training systems. Representative open-weight model families, including Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen (Yang et al., 2025), and TeleChat (He et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), have improved multilingual language modeling and instruction following through large-scale pretraining and alignment with human preferences. 17 cmHC : Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction Beyond general language capabilities, DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) and the TeleChat2, TeleChat2.5, and T1 series (Wang et al., 2025) demonstrate the role of post-training and reinforcement learning in strengthening mathematical reasoning and code generation. At the architectural and systems levels, sparse mixture-of-experts models and optimized distributed training have enabled further scaling, as illustrated by Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), DeepSeek-V4 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), and TeleChat3-MoE (Liu et al., 2025). More recent efforts increasingly coordinate architectural design with execution efficiency: DeepSeek-V4 combines compressed attention with manifold-constrained hyper-connections, while Xing4 (Song et al., 2026) jointly develops model architectures, training infrastructure, and reasoning and agentic post-training on domestic chips and frameworks. Together, these developments motivate stable and efficient architectural components for large-scale models, providing the broader context for our study of residual-stream mixing in hyper-connections. Multi-stream residual connections. Hyper-Connections (Zhu et al., 2025) extend residual connections (He et al., 2016) with learnable aggregation, mixing, and redistribution across multiple streams. To stabilize residual propagation, mHC (Xie et al., 2026) constrains residual mixing to doubly stochastic matrices through Sinkhorn normalization, while mHC-lite (Yang and Gao, 2026) uses convex combinations of permutation matrices for an exact doubly stochastic constraint. There are also improvements focusing on the efficiency of computing and scalability on more streams, such as Kronecker decomposition (Zhou et al., 2026), tensorization (Gu et al., 2026) and sparse stream update (Zhang et al., 2026). We discuss the mixing effectiveness of manifold-constrained hyperconnections, as existing research has revealed their under-mixing phenomenon, also referred to as stream collapse (Alimaskina et al., 2026) or identity degradation (Liu et al., 2026); this harms the expressivity of multi-stream design. Exploration of the Birkhoff polytope. line of recent work explores expansions of the Birkhoff polytope to address under-mixing. For example, Liu et al. (2026) constrain the residual matrices into spectral sphere which expands the doubly stochastic constraint to the negative domain. Guo et al. (2026) constrain residual matrices to 𝑆𝑂(𝑛) rotation groups and parameterizes 𝑆𝑂(4) using pairs of unit quaternions. However, such expansions cannot strictly guarantee positive mixing effect inside the Birkhoff polytope without provable stream mixing bounds. Another line of work focuses on wider feasible region inside the Birkhoff polytope to encourage interior exploration. For example, Alimaskina et al. (2026) recommend non-symmetric initialization to unbind residual matrices from the polytope vertices; Lyubinin (2026) covers the polytope with recursive transport construction; Dandachi and Diggs-Galligan (2026) and Sengupta et al. (2026) introduce the orthogonal constraint to expand the spectral reach and ensure the stability of the gradient spectrum of hyper-connections. However, these approaches often rely on more involved constructions and parameterizations, such as Cayley Transform and per-stream scaling vectors, while our approach introduces NO additional parameters and specialized constructions at all. Moreover, the effectiveness of most existing approaches is not validated on extremely large-scale model pretraining. To our knowledge, the largest parameter scale used for research-based manifoldconstrained hyper-connections is 28B by Zhang et al. (2026), while we conduct scalability tests on 300B mixture-of-experts model to validate the effectiveness and training stability of our method. Stream similarity and over-mixing. recent empirical analysis (Peng et al., 2026) shows that high representational similarity between streams does not imply functional interchangeability, as the non-redundant part of streams can still play asymmetric roles to model predictions. Our work examines different question: we study stream differences through the convergence of residual cmHC : Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction mixing and the resulting risk of over-mixing. Besides, our concern is that residual mixing can drive streams toward identical states, rather than merely making their representations similar. When streams become nearly identical to each other, the redundancy between streams can be amplified and the informative asymmetry can be weakened. C. Proofs C.1.
